item.title: Stopgaps no answer to gas crisis. [ thefinancialexpress ]
item.description:
By SYED FATTAHUL ALIM

Gas produced from rice husk as well as coal as alternative to natural gas for industries is at present under active consideration of some government leaders. Emphasis is also being laid on raising solar generation to 10,000 MW so it may support the national grid and, with storage, meet evening peak demand. Such a proposal comes at a time when factories are struggling with low gas pressure and load-shedding has also returned. As reports go, a garment factory at Dhuptara in Narayanganj is producing gas from rice husk and meeting around 70 per cent of its requirement. But the gas costs twice as much as grid gas. Now, does this offer a national solution, or merely show what a desperate factory will do to keep running?

Rice husk is no doubt a valuable biomass. Through gasification, it is heated with restricted air to produce a combustible fuel called producer gas. This can be used in boilers and for some industrial heating. But producer gas is not the same as pipeline-quality natural gas in energy content or convenience. The technology requires gasifiers, cleaning systems and trained operators to handle tar, ash and other by-products. More importantly, a factory has to secure an uninterrupted stream of husk. Paddy is harvested and milled in cycles, while its husk already has competing uses in parboiling, briquette-making, poultry bedding and household fuel. Its low bulk density makes transport and storage costly. Studies have therefore found such projects most feasible beside large rice-mill clusters where the raw material is locally available.

In that case, the Dhuptara experiment is important, but its lesson should not be overstated. Paying twice the grid-gas price may make sense when the alternative is missing an export deadline, losing buyers and leaving workers idle. Yet an emergency premium cannot become the normal energy cost of industry. Small and medium factories would be unable to buy expensive gasification equipment or maintain large husk stocks. The government may support pilot projects, common facilities in industrial clusters and research into other agricultural residues. Even so, rice husk should be treated as a local stopgap or supplementary fuel, not a universal substitute for natural gas.

The commerce  minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir's emphasis in this regard on solar power is, on the other hand, well-taken. Solar electricity cannot directly replace gas in every furnace, boiler or industrial process. But every megawatt generated from sunlight can reduce gas burnt in power plants and release more for productive industries. Solar already constitutes the overwhelming share of the country's renewable capacity, though the total remains small beside conventional generation. Reaching 10,000 MW as suggested by the minister would require an unprecedented expansion of rooftop systems, utility-scale parks, transmission facilities and battery storage. Factories, warehouses, schools and government buildings have idle roofs. These should become the first fields of the solar drive, since rooftop generation does not compete with scarce agricultural land.

Coal may similarly free some gas from power generation in the short run. However, replacing one imported fuel with another cannot be called energy security. Coal carries a heavy burden of pollution and carbon emissions, apart from exposure to international prices and shipping disruptions. In fact, no single alternative will rescue Bangladesh. 

According to the Energy Division, the country is supplying roughly 2,600 to 2,750 million cubic feet of gas a day against the 3,800 million cubic feet required to meet the shortage. Domestic fields now provide only around 1,600 million cubic feet daily. The government has plans to drill or re-drill 150 wells, connect Bhola gas with the national grid and invite international companies into offshore exploration. These plans must be pursued with deadlines, transparent contracts, modern seismic surveys and public reporting of results. Exploration carries risk and a discovery cannot start feeding factories overnight. But continued dependence on costly LNG and makeshift fuels carries a greater risk to employment, exports and foreign-exchange reserves. Rice husk may help some factories survive the present emergency and solar power can release gas for industry, but only an all-out search for new domestic gas reserves can provide a sustainable answer to the chronic crisis.

A worrying sign for remittance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The nearly 21% month by month drop in inward remittances through mobile financial services (MFS) in June should be seen as a potential warning sign that our expat workers may not be finding it feasible to send their remittance through formal channels.
For an economy that relies so heavily on remittance inflows to stabilize foreign exchange reserves, support household consumption, and cushion external shocks, it is imperative that we do all we can to make it simpler for expat workers to send their money home.
Remittances are one of Bangladesh’s most dependable economic lifelines and when they fall, the impact is immediate: Families struggle, rural economies slow, and pressure on the balance of payments intensifies.
At a time when our country is already navigating inflation, dollar shortages, and a fragile external sector, any decline should compel policy-makers to take notice.
While we agree with experts that this is no time to sound alarm bells, and that remittance earnings may yet revert back to the highs we have become accustomed to over the past two years, it is still imperative that migrant workers are shielded from the high transfer costs, inconsistent incentives, and bureaucratic hurdles that push many toward informal channels.
When formal systems become less attractive or less reliable, remittances slip underground and deprive the economy of much‑needed foreign currency.
Ensuring stable remittance flows requires a combination of streamlined digital transfer systems and stronger outreach to migrant communities. It also demands continuous coordination between banks, MFS providers, and regulators to make formal channels faster, cheaper, and more trustworthy.
Our long‑term economic stability depends on protecting this vital source of income. Bangladesh must continue to do all it can to build confidence in formal remittance channels and ensure that the earnings of migrant workers continue to strengthen the nation.

item.title: Envisioning a modern aviation sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat stating that the government is working to hold the soft opening of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s (HSIA) third terminal on December 16 is an encouraging sign for Bangladesh’s aviation sector.
It is a moment worth acknowledging not only because the terminal itself will be a modern, much‑needed upgrade, but because it hopefully signals a broader shift in how the country treats aviation - as a strategic national priority rather than an afterthought.
Bangladesh’s airports have struggled with congestion, outdated infrastructure, and service limitations that have held back both passenger experience and economic potential. For a nation with the aspirations we have, this simply will not do.
With rising demand for travel, expanding trade routes, and a growing expatriate population, the need for a modern aviation ecosystem has never been clearer.
Aviation is no longer just a luxury. Better airports mean smoother travel, stronger tourism, faster cargo movement, and improved global connectivity. They help exporters reach markets more efficiently, support foreign investment, and play a major role to enhance Bangladesh’s reputation as a country ready to compete in a globalized world.
As such, completing and inaugurating the third terminal must only be the beginning.
What Bangladesh needs is sustained investment in aviation, from upgrading regional airports to improving air traffic management, expanding cargo facilities, and ensuring that ground services meet international standards.
The country also needs better training, stronger regulatory capacity, and long‑term planning that anticipates future demand rather than reacts to crises.
That the minister has acknowledged this need is a positive sign, but this acknowledgement must now translate into tangible action.
A modern aviation sector is essential for a modern economy, and every step toward improving our airports is a step toward a more connected, competitive, and confident Bangladesh.

Türkiye must stop remembering South Asia through Pakistan alone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In June 2026, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described his visit to Dhaka as a first step towards raising Türkiye-Bangladesh relations to a strategic level. The two sides agreed on regular ministerial consultations, discussed trade and joint production, and signed an agreement on protecting cultural heritage.
A month later, Bangladesh’s army chief visited Türkiye to examine defence facilities and discuss training and technology exchange. Government ties are plainly moving forward. Turkish public awareness has not kept pace.
Pakistan occupies a special place in Türkiye’s view of South Asia. It is routinely called a brother country (“kardeş ülke” in Turkish), and that affection is neither artificial nor misplaced.
The problem is the silent assumption that Pakistan alone inherited the subcontinent’s historical solidarity with Türkiye. It did not.
When Muslims in British India supported the Turkish War of Independence, neither Pakistan nor Bangladesh existed. Bengalis were part of that mobilization.
Türkiye should therefore stop remembering South Asian Muslim support through Pakistan alone and build a reciprocal social relationship with Bangladesh, centred on historical memory, students and culture.
South Asian Muslims, including Bengalis, supported the national struggle. Bangladesh has preserved that connection unusually well. Its national poet, Kazi Nazrul Islam, wrote “Kamal Pasha” in 1921 in admiration of Mustafa Kemal. The poem entered the school curriculum. Roads in Dhaka and Chittagong carry Atatürk’s name; so do a park, a school, and a Turkish-language centre. Bangladesh has placed Türkiye in its poetry, classrooms, and public space.
The reverse is much harder to see. Bengali participation in the wider Indian Muslim campaign for Türkiye is rarely present in Turkish popular accounts. The aid is often remembered, retrospectively, as a story of Türkiye and Pakistan.
That reading compresses the geography of British India into the borders created in 1947 and treats the eastern Muslim population as an afterthought.
Pakistan and Bangladesh are not equally close to Türkiye in every policy field, nor must they be. But present-day diplomatic intensity should not determine who is allowed into historical memory.
There are understandable reasons for Pakistan’s greater visibility. Ankara and Islamabad have sustained conspicuous political, military, and diplomatic cooperation over decades. Pakistan also acts more visibly in regional security debates that attract Turkish attention.
Bangladesh has generally pursued a quieter international profile, and bilateral relations have experienced political friction, notably over the legacy of its 1971 independence.
These differences explain why Pakistan commands more attention. They do not justify turning a shared pre-partition history into an exclusively Pakistani inheritance.
This distinction matters now because official relations with Dhaka are becoming more ambitious.
Türkiye is expanding defense, trade, and humanitarian cooperation, while continuing substantial work connected to the Rohingya crisis.
Yet a relationship built mainly by ministries, defense firms, and relief agencies can remain socially thin.
Bangladesh risks appearing in Türkiye only as a market, a distant humanitarian setting or an adjunct to wider South Asian politics. Strategic language will not correct that imbalance by itself.
Turkish television has already shown how quickly cultural familiarity can grow in the other direction. Bangla-dubbed Turkish dramas have attracted mass audiences in Bangladesh; “ Kara Sevda ” reportedly captivated millions, while broadcasters developed dedicated teams of translators, scriptwriters, and voice artists.
Demand has also encouraged interest in the Turkish language. This is a major advantage, but it is still largely one-way. Bangladeshis are learning Turkish names, histories, and social codes through entertainment. Turkish audiences are learning little about Bengali life in return.
The next stage should not be another campaign that merely exports Türkiye more efficiently.
Turkish and Bangladeshi broadcasters could commission documentaries and co-productions on Kazi Nazrul Islam, Bengali support for Türkiye during the early 1920s, contemporary student life, migration, food, music, and urban change.
Turkish platforms could acquire Bangladeshi films and dramas with proper Turkish subtitles. Publishers and universities could support translations of Bengali fiction and political thought. Bangladesh’s embassy and cultural institutions also have work to do: Visibility in Türkiye cannot be produced by Ankara alone.
Bangladeshi students in Turkish universities offer the most immediate bridge. In June 2026, Bangladesh’s ambassador and Türkiye’s Presidency for Turks Abroad and Related Communities discussed expanding scholarships, training, leadership programs, and cultural exchange.
That conversation should move beyond counting scholarship recipients. Universities could fund student-led exhibitions on shared history, school visits, translation workshops, and public discussions involving Turkish classmates.
Graduates returning to Bangladesh should be connected with Turkish alumni, businesses, and cultural organizations.
Students should be supported as participants, not treated as unpaid instruments of diplomacy.
None of this requires a grand new bureaucracy. The recently signed cultural heritage agreement provides a practical opening.
A modest joint translation fund, an annual rotating public culture forum, and university grants for collaborative projects would be enough to begin.
Turkish museums, textbooks, and commemorative programs dealing with aid from Indian Muslims should explicitly include Bengal.
One accurate paragraph in a widely used exhibition may do more for mutual recognition than another official declaration of brotherhood.
Some will argue that public closeness cannot be engineered and that Pakistan’s position reflects decades of lived relations. That is partly true. Affection cannot be ordered by a ministry.
But public memory is never entirely spontaneous and is shaped by curricula, television, translations, scholarships, and commemorations. Bangladesh’s continued remembrance of Atatürk proves the point.
Giving Bangladesh a more visible place would not diminish Pakistan. Brotherhood is not a fixed quantity that one country loses when another is recognized.
The choice, then, is not between Pakistan and Bangladesh. It is between a narrow, state-centred memory of South Asia and a more accurate one.
Ankara and Dhaka are already giving their relationship strategic content. They should now give it a social foundation, beginning with the Bengalis who supported Türkiye before either modern South Asian state existed.
Until Türkiye recognizes that inheritance publicly and reciprocates Bangladesh’s cultural attention, its language of historical brotherhood will remain incomplete.
Mehmet Enes Beşer is a researcher focusing on ASEAN. His work examines Türkiye’s relations with Southeast Asian countries, particularly in the fields of economic development, industrial cooperation, and foreign policy. He's also a member of the Editorial Board of Teori magazine.

item.title: Money in the pocket, audacity on the street. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There was a time in Bangladesh when social hierarchy was strictly dictated by the optics of wealth, lineage, and unquestioned authority.
If a member of the urban upper-middle class lost their temper and berated a street vendor, a domestic worker, or a rickshaw puller, the response was almost universally a stoic, downturned gaze.
Subservience was not merely a cultural expectation; it was an economic survival strategy.
To talk back was to risk losing one’s daily bread with zero safety net waiting on the other side. Silence was the price of survival.
Fast forward through two and a half decades of relentless economic evolution, massive expansion in export-oriented manufacturing, and the explosive growth of the informal and service sectors.
The scene on a bustling Dhaka street today looks markedly different.
When an affluent driver leans out of an SUV window to deliver a condescending lecture to a ride-sharing biker or a transport worker, the response is rarely meek silence.
It is far more likely to be a sharp, immediate, and equally vocal retort.
The lower and lower-middle classes have not suddenly vaulted into upper-income brackets, nor have they escaped the modern squeezes of inflation.
Yet, their everyday social posture has fundamentally shifted.
The long-standing silence has broken because the underlying financial calculus changed.
When a person carries even a modest degree of independent financial security, their threshold for enduring personal indignity vanishes.
The theoretical engine
This shift -- where incremental gains in real income yield a radical leap in everyday self-assertion -- reflects a profound realignment that can be mapped across economics, sociology, and political philosophy.
In economic sociology, Albert O Hirschman famously conceptualized how individuals react to unfair conditions through the dynamic of exit, voice, and loyalty.
Historically, domestic helpers or manual labourers in Bangladesh were trapped in strict loyalty because the option to exit simply did not exist.
Alternative livelihoods were scarce, and losing a patron meant immediate crisis. The economic trajectory of the last 25 years altered that equation entirely.
The growth of the readymade garment (RMG) industry, logistics networks, ride-sharing platforms, food delivery, and mobile financial services created an expanded, fluid labour market.
If a worker faces verbal abuse today, the ability to walk away -- the option to exit -- is real and viable.
That underlying freedom to leave instantly alters the dynamic of voice, providing the capacity to speak back without facing immediate catastrophe.
French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu provided another angle through his analysis of capital, distinguishing between economic capital (money and assets) and cultural capital (formal education and elite social mannerisms).
Historically, elite dominance relied on holding an absolute monopoly over both, ingraining a structural habit of deference in the working class.
Today, while an industrial supervisor or delivery driver may lack elite cultural capital, their economic capital has crossed an agency threshold.
Possessing liquid cash strips away the mystical aura of upper-class superiority; a Taka holds the exact same purchasing power at the local shop regardless of who hands it over.
Philosophically, this marks the erosion of Antonio Gramsci’s cultural hegemony, as higher real wages and technology access have unraveled the working class's passive consent to elite authority.
Regional context
When placed against regional neighbours, this Bangladeshi evolution takes on an intriguing character.
Take India and Pakistan, where feudal lineage, deep-seated caste hierarchies, and agrarian landowning power structures still cast a long shadow over every-day social interactions.
In parts of rural or semi-urban South Asia, a lower-class worker's subordination is enforced not merely by current wealth, but by centuries of entrenched social rank that money alone cannot easily wipe away.
In Pakistan's feudal belts or India's stratified interior, talking back to a social superior carries risks that extend far beyond losing a day's wage -- it can invite severe extra-economic retaliation.
In contrast, Bangladesh’s rapid post-1991 economic trajectory largely bypassed traditional feudalism, leaning heavily into a mass-market, wage-labour model driven by female-led garment employment, microfinance, and massive informal urbanization.
The Bangladeshi lower class found direct liquidity before traditional social hierarchies could formalize a modern caste-like grip.
Looking east toward Southeast Asia reveals another contrast. In countries like Vietnam or Thailand, economic empowerment among the working class evolved through different structural engines.
Thailand’s lower and lower-middle classes translated their growing economic weight into organized political voice decades ago, though social deference remains heavily codified by deep-rooted cultural and institutional norms.
In Vietnam, rapid export-led industrialization drastically raised the baseline standard of living, yet labor mobility and social assertiveness are heavily mediated through formal state structures and collectivist social organization rather than individualist friction on the street.
The Bangladeshi experience is uniquely chaotic and immediate.
Without a rigid feudal caste hierarchy holding it down from the past, or strong state-mandated social frameworks guiding it from above, empowerment in Dhaka or Chittagong manifests as raw market agency.
It is an unscripted, highly individualistic democratizing force happening in real time at bus stops, tea stalls, and traffic intersections.
The new safety net
Consider how the structure of work itself enabled this specific brand of assertiveness.
In the early 1990s, lower-class employment was overwhelmingly tied to singular, informal arrangements -- manual rickshaw pulling, agricultural u, or live-in household service -- where a worker was entirely dependent on the whims of a single master.
Financial transactions were unbanked and reliant on informal advances.
Contemporary Bangladesh presents a completely different landscape.
Today's working class operates across a diversified ecosystem of garment factories, gig-economy platforms, formal logistics, and micro-enterprises.
Mobile financial services have digitized savings and peer-to-peer transfers, providing immediate cash access without needing to beg an employer for an advance.
Furthermore, household incomes are frequently hedged by remittances from abroad or secondary family earnings.
This multi-layered safety net dramatically increases a worker's risk tolerance, giving them the confidence to push back against mistreatment without fearing instant ruin.
None of this implies that structural inequality has been dismantled, or that the working class no longer faces steep hardships in healthcare, housing, or social mobility.
A bus assistant or a factory line worker remains vulnerable to broader macroeconomic shocks and cost-of-living pressures, staying anchored within the same broad social class.
Yet, the nature of daily human interaction has been permanently rewritten.
Money in the pocket acts as a psychological shield. It transforms passive endurance into active dignity.
When personal survival is no longer strictly contingent on taking insult from an affluent neighbour or patron, the old social contract collapses.
On the modern Bangladeshi street, deference is no longer given away out of fear -- it has to be earned, because the person on the receiving end finally has the leverage to talk back.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

Pakistan to host South Asian Games in April next year. [ dawn ]
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan will host the South Asian Games from April 3 to 11 next year, 23 years after it last staged the regional sports gala in Islamabad in 2004.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the South Asia Olympic Council held here on Sunday, with Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) president Arif Saeed, who is also president of the South Asian Olympic Committee, in the chair.

The meeting reviewed preparations for the Games and approved three host cities — Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar.

Representatives from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka attended the meeting in person, while India participated through video link. All the representatives endorsed the proposed dates, according to sources.

A visiting delegation is scheduled to inspect proposed sporting venues in Islamabad on Monday.

The Games will feature 28 sports and 346 medal events, with more than 3,200 athletes expected to participate across the three host cities. A large number of technical officials will also be part of the event, with Pakistan preparing to host around 4,000 athletes and other foreign visitors.

During Sunday’s meeting, representatives of the participating countries reviewed preparations and measures being taken by Pakistan to host the regional event.

The federal government has already given the go-ahead to the POA and other stakeholders to hold the Games and announced that the required funds would be released.

Pakistan was originally scheduled to host the Games in 2021, but the event was subsequently postponed for various reasons. Preparations are now said to be in their final stages.

The visiting delegation also visited the Taxila Museum and other historical sites on Sunday.

Sources said the Capital Development Authority (CDA), on the direction of the federal government, had started preparations to provide accommodation and other facilities to foreign visitors arriving in Islamabad next year for the South Asian Games and other international events, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) conference.

“The federal government has been taking every possible step to make the three international events next year in Islamabad highly successful — the South Asian Games, SCO conference and a meeting of the OIC,” a senior government official told Dawn.

He said the POA, Foreign Office and federal government were monitoring preparations to ensure that the Games were hosted successfully.

“Everyone is on board and working as a team for these Games,” he said.

Asked about India’s participation, the official said its representative had joined Sunday’s meeting through video link and endorsed the dates, which, according to him, indicated that India intended to participate.

However, another source cautioned that India’s participation could not yet be confirmed.

“India has been mixing politics with sports and has avoided visiting Pakistan. Even recently, it did not participate in a volleyball event,” the source said.

Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026
